title: Proposition 41: Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues from State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.

context.text: Placed on the ballot by petition signatures (citizen initiative), per the Official Voter Information Guide. Its text states that conflicting measures on the same ballot are void if this measure receives more affirmative votes; the opposing argument says it targets Proposition 40.

question.text: PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT. Prohibits any new state taxes that exclude their revenues from the state spending limit approved by voters in 1979. For statewide special taxes, requires (1) a pre-election audit of programs that would receive funding from a voter-proposed special tax, and (2) recurring audits of programs funded by special taxes enacted after January 1, 2026. States that other voter-approved measures appearing on the same ballot are void if they conflict with this measure and this measure receives more affirmative votes.

summary.text: Requires the State Auditor to review programs that would receive money from a voter-initiated special tax (after proponents collect 25 percent of needed signatures), with a summary printed in the Voter Information Guide if the initiative qualifies, and to audit programs funded by special taxes created or increased after January 1, 2026 every four years. It also provides that the state might not be able to exclude new special tax spending from the state appropriations limit. Fiscal impact per the Legislative Analyst: Auditor costs likely in the low millions per year, mostly paid from the new tax revenue; printing and mailing costs of a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative; possible savings if audit recommendations are implemented; net effect unknown.

measure.yesMeans: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
measure.noMeans: The California State Auditor's responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.

argumentsFor.text: Official argument in favor, signed by Denise LeDuc Froemming, CPA (CalCPAs), Tom Hayes (former California State Auditor) and Robert Gutierrez (California Taxpayers Association): "Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct performance and financial audits of the programs funded by new tax measures, with the results posted publicly."

Same argument: Prop. 41 "doesn't raise taxes" and "requires all taxes to comply with the state's voter-approved spending limit—including its requirement that excess revenues get refunded to taxpayers."

argumentsAgainst.text: Official argument against, signed by Suzanne Jimenez (SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West): "Prop. 41 isn't about auditing new taxes. It's about defeating one specific tax" (Proposition 40, the one-time tax on billionaires).
Same author's rebuttal: "it would cost the state time and money." Only one signer, SEIU-UHW, appears on the argument against.
